course.title: Digital Literacy, Cybersecurity and Responsible Technology
course.description: Builds practical digital competence, cybersecurity awareness, privacy judgement, accessibility and responsible use of technology for study and work.

outcomes.text: Organize, protect and retrieve digital information using reliable file, cloud and backup practices.
Assess digital sources, collaboration tools and online interactions for reliability, privacy and appropriate use.
Apply core cybersecurity practices including strong authentication, phishing resistance, updates and incident response.
Evaluate technology choices for privacy, accessibility, copyright, wellbeing and environmental impact.
Design a personal digital-resilience plan and demonstrate safe, accessible digital collaboration.

lessons.title: Files, formats, cloud storage and backups
objectives: Explain the difference between sync and backup
lessons.teaching_material: Digital organization is an information-management problem, not merely a naming preference. Stable folder structures, meaningful filenames, version identifiers and consistent formats reduce accidental loss and duplication. Cloud synchronization keeps copies aligned across devices but can also synchronize deletions or corruption; a true backup preserves recoverable historical copies. Sensitive material should be stored only in approved services with suitable access controls, retention and recovery procedures.
lessons.activity: Design a semester file structure, naming convention and 3-2-1-style backup plan for coursework, then test recovery of one deliberately deleted practice file.

self_check.q: Why is synchronization not the same as backup?
self_check.a: A synchronized deletion or corruption may propagate to every synced copy, while a backup is intended to preserve recoverable versions.

self_check.q: What should a filename communicate?
self_check.a: Enough context such as project, document type, date or version to identify the file without opening it.

lessons.title: Digital identity, accounts and permissions
lessons.teaching_material: A digital identity is the collection of accounts, identifiers, credentials and attributes used to access services. Good practice separates personal, academic and administrative roles where appropriate and grants only the permissions needed for a task. Shared credentials destroy accountability and should be avoided. Periodic access review removes stale accounts, unused app permissions and unnecessary sharing links, reducing both privacy exposure and the impact of account compromise.
lessons.activity: Create a personal account-and-permission inventory without recording passwords; identify three permissions or dormant accounts that should be removed or reduced.

self_check.q: What is least privilege?
self_check.a: Giving a user or application only the access necessary to perform its legitimate task.

self_check.q: Why avoid shared accounts?
self_check.a: They weaken accountability, make revocation difficult and increase the impact of credential exposure.

lessons.title: Digital search and source verification
lessons.teaching_material: Efficient digital search combines precise queries, domain or file filters, date awareness and source tracing. Search-engine ranking is not a truth score, and screenshots or reposts can remove crucial context. Verification should locate the original source where possible, inspect publication date and authorship, compare independent evidence and distinguish correction from simple repetition. Reverse image or metadata tools can support verification, but conclusions should still be based on traceable evidence.
lessons.activity: Verify three circulating online claims by tracing each to an original source, recording search steps and rating confidence with reasons.

self_check.q: Why is repeated sharing not independent corroboration?
self_check.a: Many sites may be repeating the same original claim without adding new evidence.

self_check.q: What is the first verification target for a screenshot claim?
self_check.a: The original publication, record or context from which the screenshot was taken.

lessons.title: Collaboration, netiquette and digital footprints
objectives: Evaluate long-term consequences of online publication
lessons.teaching_material: Digital collaboration works best when teams agree on channels, response expectations, document ownership, version control and decision records. Tone is harder to infer online, so concise context and respectful language reduce unnecessary conflict. Digital footprints persist through archives, screenshots, logs and copies even when a post is deleted. Responsible participation therefore considers audience, permanence, consent and professional consequences before publishing or sharing information about others.
lessons.activity: Write a one-page collaboration charter for a student project covering channels, version control, meeting records, response times, conflict handling and privacy.

self_check.q: Why document team decisions?
self_check.a: It preserves shared understanding, accountability and continuity when people or circumstances change.

self_check.q: Can deleting a post guarantee it disappears?
self_check.a: No. Copies, screenshots, caches and logs may persist elsewhere.

lessons.title: Authentication, passwords and MFA
objectives: Explain how MFA reduces account-takeover risk
lessons.teaching_material: Authentication protects access by proving an identity. Unique long passwords or passphrases, preferably managed by a reputable password manager, prevent one breach from exposing many accounts. Multi-factor authentication adds a separate factor and substantially improves resilience, although phishing-resistant methods are stronger than codes that can be socially engineered. Recovery methods matter too: insecure recovery email, reused security questions or unprotected backup codes can bypass otherwise strong login controls.
lessons.activity: Create a non-sensitive authentication plan for ten account types, selecting password-manager use, MFA method and recovery protection for each.

self_check.q: Why must passwords be unique?
self_check.a: Credential reuse lets attackers use one breached password to access unrelated accounts.

self_check.q: Does MFA make phishing impossible?
self_check.a: No. Some MFA methods can still be phished or socially engineered, though they add important protection.

lessons.title: Phishing, malware, updates and incident response
objectives: Perform first-response actions after suspected compromise
lessons.teaching_material: Phishing exploits urgency, authority, fear or curiosity to cause unsafe clicks, credential disclosure or payment. Malicious files and compromised software can also introduce malware. Updates reduce exposure to known vulnerabilities, while device encryption and backups reduce consequences when devices are lost or attacked. After suspected compromise, the priority is to contain the incident, use a trusted device to change affected credentials, revoke sessions, notify the relevant institution and preserve useful evidence rather than deleting everything immediately.
lessons.activity: Work through four simulated incidents and write the first five actions you would take for each, including what evidence should be preserved.

self_check.q: What should you do before entering credentials from an unexpected message?
self_check.a: Navigate independently to the known service or verify the request through a trusted channel instead of using the message link.

self_check.q: Why preserve incident evidence?
self_check.a: Logs, messages and timestamps may be needed for investigation, recovery, reporting or fraud disputes.

lessons.title: Privacy, data minimization and consent
lessons.teaching_material: Privacy is improved when systems collect, share and retain only data necessary for a legitimate purpose. Consent is meaningful only when people understand the choice and can exercise it without deception or coercion; many processing activities also rely on legal or contractual grounds other than consent. Students should inspect app permissions, sharing defaults and retention settings, and should avoid uploading confidential institutional, client or personal data into tools that are not approved for that information.
lessons.activity: Perform a privacy review of one commonly used app: purpose, data collected, permissions, sharing, retention, deletion controls and safer configuration.

self_check.q: What is data minimization?
self_check.a: Limiting collection and use of personal data to what is necessary for the defined purpose.

self_check.q: Why is 'I clicked accept' not the whole privacy analysis?
self_check.a: Consent quality, purpose, necessity, transparency, legal basis and downstream use also matter.

lessons.title: Accessibility, copyright and open licensing
lessons.teaching_material: Accessible digital content provides structure, keyboard operability, readable contrast, meaningful link text and alternatives such as captions, transcripts and image descriptions. Copyright protects original expression; citing a work does not automatically grant permission to reproduce it. Open licenses can permit reuse under stated conditions such as attribution or share-alike. Responsible creators record the origin and license of media before publication rather than attempting to reconstruct rights information later.
lessons.activity: Audit a five-slide deck or webpage for accessibility and media rights, then repair headings, contrast, alt text, captions and attribution records as needed.

self_check.q: Does giving credit automatically make reuse lawful?
self_check.a: No. Attribution and permission are separate; the license or applicable exception must allow the reuse.

self_check.q: Why are captions useful beyond deaf or hard-of-hearing users?
self_check.a: They also support noisy environments, language learners, searchability and review.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting and technology decisions
lessons.teaching_material: Good troubleshooting isolates causes instead of changing many things at once. Define the symptom, reproduce it safely, check recent changes, test simple hypotheses, record results and reverse failed changes where possible. Technology selection should begin with user and task requirements rather than brand preference. Security, accessibility, interoperability, cost, data portability, vendor lock-in and support life are legitimate decision criteria alongside features.
lessons.activity: Troubleshoot a controlled device or software problem using a written hypothesis log, then build a weighted decision matrix comparing two tools for a study task.

self_check.q: Why change one variable at a time when troubleshooting?
self_check.a: It makes it possible to identify which change affected the problem and avoids introducing additional unknowns.

self_check.q: What is vendor lock-in?
self_check.a: Dependence on a provider that makes switching costly or difficult because of data, formats, integrations or contracts.

lessons.title: Wellbeing, sustainability and personal resilience plan
objectives: Assess digital habits for wellbeing and sustainability
lessons.teaching_material: Responsible technology use considers human wellbeing and environmental effects as well as productivity. Notification overload, poor ergonomics, sleep disruption and constant context switching can reduce performance. Device manufacture, data centers and network use also have environmental costs, so extending device life, avoiding unnecessary storage or computation and selecting efficient services can matter at scale. A resilience plan combines security, backup, privacy, accessibility and healthy-use routines into repeatable habits.
lessons.activity: Produce a personal digital-resilience plan covering account security, backups, device updates, privacy reviews, accessibility, recovery contacts, screen habits and sustainable device practices.

self_check.q: Why include recovery planning before an incident?
self_check.a: During a crisis access, evidence and decision quality may be worse, so predefined recovery steps reduce delay and error.

self_check.q: What is one sustainability benefit of extending device life?
self_check.a: It delays replacement and can reduce resource extraction, manufacturing and e-waste impacts.

assessments.title: Digital Security and Privacy Audit
assessments.instructions: Audit a fictional or sanitized student digital environment for storage, authentication, permissions, phishing exposure, updates, backups and privacy risks; submit prioritized remediation actions.

assessments.title: Accessible Digital Collaboration Project
assessments.instructions: Create a small collaborative digital artifact with documented accessibility, attribution, privacy and version-control decisions.

assessments.title: Personal Digital Resilience Plan
assessments.instructions: Submit a practical resilience plan with threat scenarios, account controls, backup/recovery, privacy review, wellbeing practices and a quarterly maintenance checklist.
